phrases: Wooded shores ring the Long Lake — pine on the steep mountain flanks and willow on the wet margins; the trees of Mirkwood's eaves come down to the water's edge.
Snow lies on the pines above the lake and the shores are rimmed with ice; the Long Lake is grey steel under white hills.
Rain mists the pines and raises the lake; the southern arms spread over their margins and the marsh-paths drown under brown water.
The ways of Esgaroth are waterways — the channels between the lake's long arms and the current of the Forest River, spanned by the wooden streets and piers of Lake-town.
The channels skin with ice at the lake's edge; the town's lanterns reflect on black water and the wooden ways creak and sway in the cold.
Rain beats on the lake and the wooden town; the channels blur, the lanterns halo in the wet, and the water rises around the piles.
On land, marshy paths skirt the lake's southern arms; on the water the ways are marked by piles and lanterns between the hidden channels.
The marsh-paths are frozen mud; the reeds are dead and white, and the lake-wind comes across the open water like a blade.
Cultivated, Mediterranean woodland: groves of holm-oak, chestnut and cypress give way to olive and almond on the warmer slopes, with orchards and flowering vales.
The undergrowth is aromatic with broom, thyme and rockrose; tended, sunlit, prosperous woods.
Fertile foothills of the White Mountains, terraced with vine and olive and laced with clear streams.
Warm and sunlit, the green skirts where mountain meets tilled land.
The high White Mountains, the Ered Nimrais, crowned with perpetual snow and glacier above the treeline.
Knife-edged ridges and sheer pale walls blaze in the sun; the cold is absolute, the silence broken only by wind and distant ice.
The green foothills of the White Mountains, terraced with olive and vine where they meet the lowlands, laced with shepherd-paths and tumbling brooks.
Warm, fertile and sunlit, the gentlest face of the great range.
The middle slopes of the Ered Nimrais, where forest yields to alpine meadow and grey crag.
Cloud snags on the ridges, streams fall in white threads, and the air thins and chills as the green runs out into stone.
The rich level fields of Gondor's most peopled land, watered by many rivers, quilted with farms and pasture between the coast and the hills.
A well-kept Gondorian road of fitted stone, straight and sure, with drainage and standing waymarks; the traffic of trade and soldiery keeps it busy and its verges clear.
A trodden countryside path between orchards and terraces, sun-warm and clear, worn smooth by shepherds and farmhands.
Sun-scorched scrubland rather than true forest: thorn, tamarisk and stunted wind-bitten oak scattered over an arid contested plateau, their roots gripping cracked red earth.
Sparse, dusty shade in a debated borderland baked between Gondor and the South.
Fertile foothills of the White Mountains, terraced with vine and olive and laced with clear streams.
Warm and sunlit, the green skirts where mountain meets tilled land.
Sun-baked open country of dune-field, dry scrub and salt-flat, shimmering and stark, rolling toward the deserts of the south.
A well-kept Gondorian road of fitted stone, straight and sure, with drainage and standing waymarks; the traffic of trade and soldiery keeps it busy and its verges clear.
A trodden countryside path between orchards and terraces, sun-warm and clear, worn smooth by shepherds and farmhands.
Sparse, wind-scoured woods on a rocky, desolate coast: stunted oak and pine bent by the sea-gales, clinging to the spurs of the White Mountains above fishing villages and gold-miners' tracks.
Few trees of size survive here; the land is harsh, salt-bitten and poor, far from Gondor's prosperous heartland.
Fertile foothills of the White Mountains, terraced with vine and olive and laced with clear streams.
Warm and sunlit, the green skirts where mountain meets tilled land.

A trodden countryside path between orchards and terraces, sun-warm and clear, worn smooth by shepherds and farmhands.
Oak and beech hangers on the down-slopes, tall and little-visited, dark yew standing in the combes.
The woods are old, but the pasture between them is older.
Foxgloves and hart's-tongue in the shady hollows.
The hangers stream in the rain; water runs down the combe-paths, and the foxgloves hang their bells heavy with wet.
Rolling chalk downs of cropped turf running west, the ridges lifting until the land smells of the sea.
Barrows and old earthworks crown the high points, and skylarks over all.
The westernmost downland before the Tower Hills.
The downs stand pale under a white sky; the earthworks and barrows are rimmed with frost, and the skylarks are gone.
High beyond the border the slate peaks of the Ered Luin hold their snow late, remote and blue — the last heights of the West, seen but not crossed.
The foothill country where the downs give way to the stone of the Ered Luin — heather and thorn between outcrops, the air resin-sharp.
The mountains begin here quietly, in broken ground and running water.
The lower flanks of the Blue Mountains west of the downs — grey slate shoulders above the stream-vales, bare and wind-scoured.
Snow lies in the gullies late into spring.
The road west to the Tower Hills and the Havens beyond — once busy with kings' business, now quiet, its milestones green with lichen.
Elves pass on it seldom, and when they do they do not hurry back.
Green lanes between the sheep-downs, over the old earthworks and under the beeches.
Paths from the Shire lands join them here and there, though the folk of the east come seldom this far.
Rain blows across the downs in veils; the green lanes run wet, the beeches drip, and the Tower Hills are lost ahead in the murk.
Oak and ash in the sheltered vales, coppice-managed by generations of smallholders, hazel and holly along the wood-edges.
The trees here are worked, not wild — timber and firewood for the barns of the heartland.
In the deeper coverts the wood thickens into old broadleaf, green shade over leaf-mould.
Rain settles through the oak and ash; the rides run wet and the leaf-mould is dark and heavy.
The coppice-smoke of the smallholders hangs low under the eaves.
The White Downs roll south in long pale swells of chalk and turf, rich and settled.
Sheep-cropped slopes between hedged fields, mill-ponds bright in the folds, waymarks and stone walls along every ridge.
The busiest land in all Arthedain.
The White Downs stand pale under frost, the turf stiff and the mill-ponds skinned with ice.
From the ridges the smoke of every farmstead stands straight in the still air.
Rushy bottoms and sedge-flats along the streams that feed the Baranduin — wet ground claimed from the field and left to the heron and the snipe.
Mill-leats run straight and dark between the reeds.
In the wet years the flats go under and the mills stand idle.
A busy farm-road of the heartland, wheel-rutted and hedge-lined, running between market villages that are never more than an hour apart.
Drove-lanes join it from the sheep-walks; on market days the carts of wool and grain keep it loud.
A field-path over stiles and through gaps in the hedge, worn by farmhands and wandering folk.
Cottages and byres show beyond every rise, and a chimney is never far off.
Blackberries thicken the hedges in season.
The safest walking in the north-kingdom.
Frost holds the ruts hard underfoot; the stiles are white-rimmed and the breath smokes.
The downs go pale and silent under a low sun.
Rain sits soft on the heartland; the field-paths run with brown water, the hedges drip, and every farm chimney smokes into the wet.
A mixed land more than a wood: fertile lowland plains and pasture broken by ragged copses of oak and birch, the thinned remnant of older forest.
Harsh winds scour the uplands while the river-vales lie green and tilled, dotted with the heath and bracken reclaiming abandoned ground.
Low chalk-and-turf downs rolling to the horizon, dotted with ancient barrows and crowned here and there by weathered stone.
Open, windswept, and brooding over the old graves.
Wide degraded lowlands of heath and rough pasture, the felled and half-empty plain where great forest once stood, rolling flat toward the sea.

A weathered stretch of the Great North Road, once proud and now patched and rutted, its milestones toppled; still used by merchant caravans that move in numbers, wary of the empty leagues between towns.
A faint field-path through heath and old pasture, easy to lose where the bracken has swallowed it, threading between grass-grown barrows.
Dark, storm-twisted oakwood clinging to a wind-scoured coastal cape, dense and salt-bitten, sheltering an ancient folk apart from the world.
A brooding, silent wood under sea-grey skies.
No road worth the name; only a treacherous trace through the dark wood and its poisoned mires, known to the Woses and shunned by all others.
A perilous thread through the twisted wood, marked by Wose-signs a stranger cannot read, skirting the mires where worse things wait.
Woods of resinous fir, cedar and cypress clothe the broken hills, set among broad glades where herbs and heath grow thick.
The air is fresh and sweet, and recalls fairer countries far to the north.
Soft rain falls on the herb-glades and the resinous woods; the air is washed and sweet, and every bush drips with a sharper scent.
Green broken hills rolling down toward the Anduin — a fair land gone half-wild, where old gorse blooms gold on the scarred slopes and bay, thyme and sage fill the hollows with scent.
The gorse blazes gold on the warm hillsides; the sun draws up the smell of thyme and cedar, and the whole land hums with bees.
The glades are grey and the heath is bent low; frost lies in the sheltered hollows, but the air keeps a memory of herbs.
The old South Road winds down toward the cross-roads and the ruined bridges of Osgiliath — grass-grown now, and shadowed where it nears the eastern vale.
The South Road lies pale and empty under a cold sky; frost whitens its verges and the woods stand black along its edges.
Hidden paths thread the thicket and the glade — the ways of rangers among the gorse and myrtle, running to lookouts above the river and the forbidden pools.
The hidden paths run soft and wet; rain patters on the gorse, and the herbs give up their scent to the wet air.
The dark fir-wood of the Dimholt clings to the mountain's root — black trees that seem untouched by light, where old stones stand in rows like sentinels before a hidden door.
The black trees of the Dimholt are rimed and still; frost fills the hollow between the ancient stones, and the dark beyond the door seems to breathe the cold.
Green upland pastures above the Morthond vale, falling away in steep grassy slopes to the black river below.
The southern cliffs rise sheer beyond, like a wall of stone.
Snow lies on the high pastures and the vale runs grey beneath it; lights begin to flicker early in the dwellings below.
The high snows stand remote and bright; at their feet the mountain's shadow fills the upper vale through most of the day, and the cold comes down before the light goes.
The high peaks are a wall of winter; their snow reaches down to the black wood, and the vale below is a grey pool of dusk.
The foothills of the White Mountains rise in long grassy spurs; sheep-paths wind among gorse and stone, and the high flocks graze where the air thins.
Snow fills the spurs and the sheep-paths vanish; the dark firs of the Dimholt carry it in heavy black folds.
The southern wall of Ered Nimrais towers over the vale — white peaks above the black wood of Dimholt and the dark door that no foot returns from.
The road runs up the vale beside the black water of the Morthond, passing under the shadow of the cliffs to the mountain hamlets and the high stone circles of the old folk.
Rain falls grey on the vale and the Morthond rises dark and fast; the cliffs run with thin silver threads of water.
Old paths climb the grass slopes to the high pastures; one darker track enters the Dimholt and ends at the upright stone like a warning finger, and beyond it there is no path.
A cold comes down off the high snows and pools in the upper vale; the paths are white with frost and the black wood is silent.
Scattered groves and gallery-woods of oak and willow along the streams of the wide southern grasslands, islands of shade among the horse-pastures of the Eothraim.
Open, sunlit, and loud with wind over grass.
Broad northern grasslands stretching flat to the sky, rich pasture in summer and mire in the spring thaw, loud always with wind over grass.
A grass-worn horse-track across the open plains, faint but sure to those who ride it, following the streams and the herds rather than any surveyor's line.
A rider's thread across the grass, barely there, that follows the graze of the herds and the line of the streams.

Sparse degraded woods of oak and thorn on a windswept plateau, the felled and grazed-over remnant of older forest.
Heath and bracken reclaim the gaps; bleak and half-empty.
A bleak windswept plateau of wind-flattened grass and empty distance, half-wild and all but unpeopled beneath a wide sky.
A lonely stretch of old road across the windswept plateau, its paving long since scattered, running empty between distant and half-ruined steads.
A lonely path across the empty plateau, faint in the wind-flattened grass, marked by the odd standing stone worn faceless.
Low scrub of birch and juniper clinging to the island's sheltered hollows — the canopy kept knee-high by gales that sweep the summit bare.
Puffin and guillemot own the cliffs; the wood belongs to the lee side.
A half-forgotten Elf-way circling the island above the sea — grey stone where the ground allows, bare rock where the wind scoured it away.
The island's cliff-paths thread between the bird-ledges and the spray; below, hidden coves open and shut in the tide.

Stunted pine and birch clinging to dark, ore-streaked slopes, sparse and hardy.
The wood gives out fast into rugged dwarf-mined stone; the air smells of iron and cold.
Low rugged ridges of dark ore-bearing stone, scarred with dwarf-mines and old roads, hard and treeless and smelling of iron.
The lower slopes of the Iron Hills, dark with ore-bearing rock and dwarf-delvings, ridged and rugged but not lofty, the wind smelling of iron and cold stone.
A hard dwarf-road of dressed stone, straight and enduring, cut for ore-wagons between the delvings, ringing under iron-shod wheels.
A stony miner's path between the delvings, blazed with chisel-marks on the rock, hard and sure though never gentle.
Woodlands of pine and rowan clothe the lower valley — young growth on old burnt land, where the Desolation of the Dragon once spread grey ash for miles around the Mountain.
The young woods are green and loud with birds; the Mountain's shadow lies cool across the valley floor, and the river runs bright between the banks.
Snow lies on the young woods and the Mountain's flanks; the valley is white and still, and the ravens croak on the bare ridge above the gate.
Rain sweeps the long valley; the young pines shine dark and the grey scars of the old desolation run with black water.

The road runs up the long valley to the Front Gate of Erebor beside the River Running — a way remade and busy again, where the realm of the dwarves and the town of Dale keep their watch and their trade.
The road to the Gate runs white and cold beside the ice-rimmed river; the Mountain's peak stands over it like a white crown on a grey throne.
Paths climb the bare slopes about the Mountain — stony ways where the old scars of the desolation are still carved in the rock, and the raven-guards watch from the bare ridge of Ravenhill.
Snow fills the ravines and hides the paths; the broken slopes about the Mountain are a white maze of rock and drift.
The stony paths are white lines between black rocks; the wind off the Mountain is bitter, and the heights above are deep in drifted snow.
The deep green oakwoods of the Green-elves — sessile oak and hazel, moss-bearded, fern-floored, rain-fed by the west wind.
Red deer move in them unbothered, and the Elves who dwell there pass like weather through the trees.
These are the old rain-woods of Lindon, dripping and dim and very old.
The rain-wood is built for this — rain drips from the moss-bearded oaks, the ferns shine black-green, and the deer stand quiet under the boughs.
The wood-road north toward the Gulf runs dim beneath the canopy, its stones soft with leaf-mould.
The Elves keep it more by passing than by mending.
Light falls in green shafts where the way bends to the streams.
Deer-paths and wood-ways between the glades, marked only by those who dwell within — a notch, a bent branch, a stone set just so.
The unlettered traveller finds them gentle and endlessly wandering.
Rain works its way through the canopy for hours after it falls; the wood-ways run soft and the moss drinks it all.
The oakwoods stand grey and dripping in the mild dark of winter; the wood-ways are soft underfoot, and the glades keep their green.
Tall pines and green oakwoods on the seaward slopes of the Blue Mountains, standing since the Elder Days — the last living margin of a land the Sea drowned.
Resin-sharp and mossy-floored, quiet as held breath.
Rain comes in off the Sea in long veils; the woods drip and the mosses drink, and the air smells of salt and wet pine.
The green woods stand dark and wet under the sea-wind; frost is rare here, but the rain of the western winter is long and cold.
Heather moors and grey slate ridges rising out of the pinewoods — the first shoulders of the Blue Mountains, cold-streamed and open to the sky.
Old delvings scar the scree; the Dwarves' halls are long silent.
Snow lies on the blue ridges and the gulf-wind is bitter; the Sea below is grey as iron and the hills are white above it.
The bare blue backs of the range — wind-scoured slate heights where the snow lies late into spring.
The stone itself is blue-grey, and the silence on it is older than kingdoms.
Snow lies long on the high moors; the blue stone shows through it in bands, and the wind off the Sea is edged with ice.
The road to the Grey Havens runs west along the gulf — a white way ending at the quays where the swan-prowed ships wait for the last sailing.
The road to the Havens runs under a grey sky beside a grey gulf; the mountains are white above and the water dark below, and the way feels like the last way in the world.
Old dwarf-roads and elven paths thread the valleys — ways worn before the world was changed, still trodden by the dwindling folk of the mountains' halls.
Sea-rain drives across the ridges; the old paths run with water, and the mountains are a blue wall hidden in grey mist.
Wind-pruned hawthorn and stunted sycamore crouched in the cliff-top hollows, salted grey on their seaward side.
In the sheltered coombes behind the headlands small woods of oak stand greener, kept from the gale.
The cliff-top woods hiss under the rain, salt on the wind; in the coombes the oaks drip and the ferns drink.
The coast-road runs along the headlands above the surf, from cape to cape, with beacon-heights at the great promontories.
To the west the sea stands like a wall of light; the Elves walk it the way a man walks a garden-wall, looking out.
Cliff-paths dipping to seal-coves and bird-ledges, salt spray drying white on the grass.
Puffins and guillemots crowd the stacks below.
Where the path drops, the sea comes close enough to wet your feet.
Sea-rain drives across the headlands; the cliff-paths stream, the puffins are gone to sea, and the surf comes up white to meet the weather.
Winter gales strip the headlands bare; the sea runs high and grey-green, and the paths along the capes are walked by no one at all.
The great seaways of Belegaer run grey and wide under the western sky — the long lanes out of the Havens, where the swan-prowed ships take their leave of the shores of Middle-earth.
Winter seas are iron and slate; the wind is a great cold wheel out of the west, and the waves march in grey ranks to break upon the shores of Middle-earth.
Rain and sea-mist meet over the water; the horizon drowns, and the world becomes a grey wheel of wind and wet with no edge and no end.
The lesser lanes of the coast-wise sailors wind between cape and island, marked by the lights of the Havens and the wheeling of white sea-birds.
The coast-lanes in winter are ways of white water and screaming wind; the seabirds hang like blown rags and the shore is a line of foam.
Rain flattens the grey water into a beaten sheet; the coast dissolves in mist, and sea and sky are one weeping grey.
Sparse, hardy woods of pine and birch in a rugged northern wilderland, wind-bitten and thinly grown over stony ground.
A frontier forest, cold and little-trodden.
Open rough plains of coarse grass and reed between the streams, half-wild and thinly grazed under a wide grey sky.
A rough track between scattered northern steads, mud in the thaw and dust in the summer, kept open only by the passing of the folk who need it.
A muddy footpath between northern crofts, faint and rough, marked by a leaning post or a cairn where it forks.
Scattered groves of whitebeam, rowan and wild apple above the meadows, bent by the sea-wind but green to the last branch.
Birdsong fills them in season — the land's name given leaf.
Rain bends over the groves of whitebeam and rowan; the meadow-paths run wet, and the birdsong stops and starts between the showers.
The way along the sheltered bays runs between the flower-meadows and the dunes, mild and bright.
In high summer the meadows blaze with wildflowers; in grey months the light still comes off the water wide and soft.
Meadow-paths through the flowery turf — orchids and harebells underfoot, skylarks hanging over the dunes.
Gentle walking; the sea keeps pace beside you.
Soft rain blows in off the bays; the flower-meadow darkens, the dunes stream, and the wildflowers bow under the weight of the sky.
Birch and willow scrub in the wet hollows between the moors, silver-barked and thin.
On the dry ridges small pines stand old and dark.
The wood hugs the sheltered ground and leaves the heights to the heather.
The wet hollows stream; the birch and willow stand dripping over water that was paths, and the bog-cotton bends under the weather.
The moor-road runs on its causeways over the peat, dark pools to either side and the hills' shoulders beyond.
Stone-set and enduring — the Elves' work outlasting the bog it crosses.
Peat-bank paths between the heather, bog-cotton blowing white in season, the ground speaking underfoot.
Follow the high ground or follow a guide; the pools do not forgive wandering feet.
Rain comes down soft and long on the moors; the peat-pools rise, the causeways shine, and the heather is black with wet.
The moors lie dun and dark under the winter sky; the peat is soft and the pools are cold and the wind does the rest.
Tall sessile oak in the sheltered vales, with hazel, holly and rowan at the wood's hem — the tended wood of the Green-elves, kept as the Elves keep all things: lightly and forever.
Deer graze the margins unbothered.
The sessile oaks take the rain patiently; the wood drips and gleams, and the deer do not stir from the deep shelter of the hazels.
The Elf-road south toward the Tower Hills, quiet and well-kept, bordered in season by the flax-fields and vines of the serene estates.
Few mortals have ever walked it; fewer still are missed.
Green ways between the estates, along the streams and under the oak, unhurried and unmarked.
The Elves use them as much for walking as for going anywhere at all.
Rain falls mild on the estates; the flax bends, the vines drip, and the green ways between the fields run soft and quiet.
Pine and juniper on the rocky ridges above the sea-lochs, resin-sharp, rooted in stone.
Below them the grey water fills the channels between the skerries.
The pine and juniper drip cold resin-smelling rain; below them the loch-channels run grey and loud between the rocks.
The shore-road winds between the skerries, grey stone on the land side, greyer water on the sea.
Seal-heads rise in the channels to watch the wayfarer pass.
Fisherman's paths down to the boat-sounds and the mussel-shores, slick with wrack and salt.
Where they end, small boats lie hauled above the tide.
Rain hisses on the sea-lochs and beads the juniper; the skerries vanish into grey, and the boat-shores are wet and empty.
Birch, rowan and pine in the sheltered vales beneath the blue ridges — bright in autumn, loud with meltwater in spring.
The vales hold the wood; the heights hold the wind.
Rain in the vales is half river; the birch and rowan drip, the streams answer from below, and the mist sits where the wood ends.
Heather-clad shoulders of grey stone rising from the vales, cut by cold west-running streams.
Steep but never deadly, the air sharp with resin and sea-wind.
Snow lies on the shoulders above the vales; the heather shows through in dark patches, and the streams run loud beneath the ice-edges.
The high bare crests above the vales — rock breaking through the heath, wind singing in the gullies, the rubble of vanished dwarf-mansions on the scree.
The vale road runs south along the Lhun toward the Gulf and the Havens — the way the Elves take when they take their leave, and the way the deer take to the water.
Paths along the cold streams and up the spur-crests — the old valley ways between the dwarf-holds and the sea.
Rain brings the streams up loud and fast; the paths along the water are dark with wet, and the blue ridges are lost in low cloud.
Wooded shores and willow-islands crowd the River's banks; upstream the shores grow steep, and trees stand dark along the narrowing channel where the current quickens.
The wooded banks stand black and bare; mist lies along the pale margins of the water at dusk, and the rocks cast long shadows under a cold sky.
Long fenlands fringe the low western banks — reeds and sad grasses where small birds pipe and whistle, and swan-wings rush overhead at dusk.
Rain curtains the view across the River; the reeds bow, the pools blur into one grey sheet, and the far bank is a rumour and a shadow.
Open grasslands roll back from the western bank — treeless plains where a fresh breeze brings thin clouds up from the distant south, and shadows lengthen slowly at day's end.
On the treeless plain the sun climbs to noon over waving grass; thin clouds drift up from the south and shadows lengthen across the open ground.
An icy morning wind moves over the plains; the stars fade on a pale eastern sky, and the grass crackles underfoot in the growing grey light.
The River itself is the road — a broad grey flood running south between the banks, misty at dawn and hiding the far shore.
Below the rapids of Sarn Gebir the way is broken and the portage steep.
The River runs dark and high between its banks; mist lies on the water at dusk, and a cold wind follows the channel south.
Rain curtains the River; mist hides the far bank, and the channel narrows and quickens between steep grey shores until the rapids' roar comes up through the wet.
Landing-paths of trodden mud and reed thread the banks; above them stony shores rise toward wooded hills and bare uplands of grey rock.
Wooded slopes climb from the lake-shore at the field of the green lawns — groves of rowan and oak beneath the heights, where a small spring rises and falls beside the grey water.
Rain fills the springs and darkens the lawns; Rauros roars louder through the wet, and the mist of the falls mingles with low cloud.
Southward the land breaks into tangled fens before the marshes of the dead — a wilderness of reeds, pools and boggy ground, drear and unkind under a low sky.
A bitter east wind moves over the fens; the pools skin with ice at their edges, and the reeds hiss like steel.
The fens spread and swell in the rain; every hollow is a pool, and mist and water make a single grey country.
The River below the Falls is the way south — but the way is broken by the rapids of Sarn Gebir and the great fall of Rauros, and the portage is steep and stony.
Old paths climb from the lawns to the high seats of the hills — worn stone steps split by tree-roots, where the watchers of Gondor once looked east across the water.
The stone steps are slick with frost and the high seat stands cold and empty; below, the Falls thunder on regardless through the white land.
The west-eaves of the great Wood — oak and elm under the shadow of the deeper forest, friendlier than the black heart but still dim and watchful.
The Woodmen's halls stand in clearings hidden among them.
The oaks stand bare and the mast lies deep under frost; the clearings are white, and the smoke of the hidden halls climbs into the cold.
Rain drips through the eaves and pools on the paths; the wood smells of wet leaf and hidden smoke, and the deer stand still in the oak-shelter.
The woods are deep green and loud with bees; the meadows of the clearings stand high with grass, and the air is warm and sweet.
The forest-roads of the Woodmen run between hidden halls and the western fords of Anduin — narrow ways kept secret from the dark things of the Wood.
Paths thread the oak-woods between the clearings; red deer move on them, and the Woodmen know each mark and turning as their own hall.
The paths are drifts of leaves frozen hard; the marks of the Woodmen are sharp in the frost and the deer have gone to the sheltered glades.
The oaks stand bare and the mast lies deep under the leaves; frost whitens the ford-stones and the River runs dark and cold.
The vales are loud with bees; the oakwoods are deep green, and the high grass of the meadows stands ready for the scythe.
Great oaks and elms clothe the vales between river and mountain — the woodlands of the Beornings, deep in mast and honey, where the deer and the bees have more right than any stranger.
The Gladden Fields lie silent under frost — brown reeds, black pools, and the thin cry of a single bird over the wide water.
Reed-beds and fen-pools spread where the streams leave the mountains — the Gladden Fields, quiet under the sky and whispering of a doom long past.
Rain swells the ford until the stepping-stones run just awash; the mountains hide behind grey cloud and the River is loud between the banks.
The Old Ford and the paths of the forest road make the way; the River runs broad between the banks, and the mountains wall the west.
Snow fills the vales and caps the Carrock like a white crown; the trails are a single white line between the River and the black eaves of Mirkwood.
Trails climb from the fords to the Carrock — the great stone standing mid-river — and wind on into the vales under the eaves of the Wood.
Snow and storm rule the heights; ice falls like rain and the peaks vanish in a white fury that no traveller outfaces.
The mountain itself seems to breathe malice.
Above the cloud-line the cold is absolute — fierce sunlight on a hard summit beneath a turning sky, thin air, and the slow groan of burdened stones.
The high peaks stand above a world of cloud — cruel Caradhras, Celebdil's bare horn, and Fanuidhol's grey head.
Thunder and lightning break over them when the mountains are angry, and ice falls like rain.
Rain drives across the slopes and turns every ledge to a waterfall; the pines bend and hiss under the weight of it, and the paths are running mud.
Steep, deceptive slopes of pine and bare rock where the high country begins.
Wind, falling water, and cracking stone break the mountain silence, and the paths lie as often as they lead.
Mountain storms fill the night with sudden flashes and thunder rolling through the hollows; the ledges stream with water and the valleys below are lost in murk.
The middle slopes are buried in white silence; the pines carry it in great folds and the streams are frozen threads under the drifts.
Grey shoulders and hanging valleys between the snow-line and the woods; waterfalls leap from the cliffs and vanish into mist below, and the passes are ledges of cold stone.
The high passes climb by exposed ledges and false paths; at the crest the way narrows to a knife of stone between storms, and the Redhorn Gate keeps its own grim weather.
Winter locks the passes: the trails are deep in drifted snow, the ice on the stones is glass-hard and deadly, and the way is memory and guesswork.
Goat-paths thread the crags; below them the valleys open in glimpses of green between the pines, and the mountains cast long shadows at sunset across the hidden dales.
The black heart of the Wood — ancient oaks and beeches bent together into a gloomy arch, trunks tangled with ivy and lichen.
Beneath them a dim green light barely reveals the way; the air is thick, still and watchful, and black butterflies drift through the gloom like leaves that will not fall.
In summer the heat under the canopy is still and heavy, the air rank with spores; no breeze reaches through the interlaced boughs.
In winter the cold seeps up from the roots and frost makes strange patterns in the gloom; the black trunks stand bare and the dimness turns grey.
Rain on the eaves becomes a ceaseless drip below; the trunks run black with wet and the dim green light sinks to darkness.
The cold in the deep wood is a damp, creeping thing — it lives in the black earth and the still air, and no fire built here burns right.
The Elf-path winds east under the eaves — a narrow thread of beaten earth between black trunks.
It is the one safe way through, and straying from it is the forest's oldest trap.
Rain darkens the path to a black thread; the wood closes over it like a tunnel, and the drip of the trees is the only sound.
Within the wood the game-trails are lies — they wind among the roots and fade in the dark.
The stream that crosses them runs black and still, and it is not to be touched.
The false trails are drifts of black leaves gone stiff with frost; the dark stream is rimed at its edges and the wood is utterly still.
The tall woods stand leafless and dark against the white towers; the sea-wind brings a smell of salt up the western slopes.
Rain sweeps the western slopes; the woods hiss and drip, and the towers stand dim white shapes in the murk.
Woods of tall beech and ash standing in the gorges and on the sheltered slopes, elven-tended since the Elder Days.
Bluebells carpet them in spring; the deer come down to them at dusk.
The trees here have never been felled.
The road west runs pale under frost; the towers stand white on the hill, and beyond them the Sea is grey and near.
The pilgrim-road climbs to Elostirion on the highest crest — Elves and the Faithful of old went up it to look west, and the stones remember.
From its bends the Gulf of Lhun opens wide below, and on the clearest days a far eye might glimpse the Sea itself.
Turf paths winding up the chalk slopes between the gorges, skylarks over the cropped grass, rabbit-workings in the banks.
At the top: three white towers, and the sea.
Rain blows in off the unseen Sea; the green hills shine dark with wet and the towers are blurred above the streaming woods.
Grim, broken upland woods of stunted oak, pine and thorn strewn with mossy boulders, cold and ill-tended.
In the Trollshaws and Ettenmoors the trees shelter trolls and worse among the tumbled grey stones.
Bleak boulder-strewn moor-hills of grey rock and coarse grass, cold and trackless, where trolls den among the tumbled stones and the wind moans across empty heights.
A broken remnant of an old Dunadan road, its stones heaved apart by frost and root, half-reclaimed by heather; a grim and little-mended way where travellers are watched from the hills.
Barely a trail at all, a lost thread through the black-pine hollows, marked only by old blazes cut in the bark and half healed over by time.

Rain soaks the woods for days on end; fires will not kindle, and the dripping of the beeches goes on long after the sky has cleared.
Thick woods of beech and oak cover the broken ground, dim even at noon.
The shade is old and uneasy; travellers speak low here without knowing why.
Snow fills the hollows and the ravines; the stony paths are treacherous with ice, and the mountain wind drives flakes like ash through the trees.
The cold settles in the folds of the hills; even the streams run quieter, and the rock holds the frost long after noon.
Steep stony hills folded into ravines and hollows — troll-country, where the caves in the rock are best left unsearched and the fires seen among the trees at night are best left alone.
The Road runs wet and gloomy under streaming skies; the fords rise brown and fast, and the stone of the hills shines black with wet.
The Road climbs and winds among the hills, fording stony streams that rush down noisy and cold from the mountains; its verges are grown over and the land remembers crueller times.
Ice feathers the rocks beside the path and every breath smokes; the hollows below are pits of shadow and cold fern.
Stony paths wind downhill beside rock walls, dropping into bush-filled hollows on the far side; every turn demands a pause and a listening.

Stunted, wind-broken pine and thorn cling to cold grey slopes under perpetual cloud, snow lingering in their shadow.
A grim, sparse wood in a land that resents the living.
Cold bare hill-country under perpetual grey cloud, snow lingering in the hollows, grim and silent beneath the brooding strongholds of the Witch-king.
The cold low mountains of Angmar, bare grey rock under perpetual cloud, snow-streaked and wind-scoured, where the Witch-king's strongholds brood among the crags.
A hard-frozen war-road of grey stone kept open by slave-gangs, rutted by the passage of the Witch-king's supply caravans, watched from cold forts along its length.
A frozen track over bare grey slopes, marked by the odd heap of stones, treacherous with ice and easily lost when the cloud comes down.
Tall pines and green oakwoods on the seaward slopes of the Blue Mountains, standing since the Elder Days — the last living margin of a land the Sea drowned.
Resin-sharp and mossy-floored, quiet as held breath.
Rain comes in off the Sea in long veils; the woods drip and the mosses drink, and the air smells of salt and wet pine.
The green woods stand dark and wet under the sea-wind; frost is rare here, but the rain of the western winter is long and cold.
Heather moors and grey slate ridges rising out of the pinewoods — the first shoulders of the Blue Mountains, cold-streamed and open to the sky.
Old delvings scar the scree; the Dwarves' halls are long silent.
Snow lies on the blue ridges and the gulf-wind is bitter; the Sea below is grey as iron and the hills are white above it.
The bare blue backs of the range — wind-scoured slate heights where the snow lies late into spring.
The stone itself is blue-grey, and the silence on it is older than kingdoms.
Snow lies long on the high moors; the blue stone shows through it in bands, and the wind off the Sea is edged with ice.
The road to the Grey Havens runs west along the gulf — a white way ending at the quays where the swan-prowed ships wait for the last sailing.
The road to the Havens runs under a grey sky beside a grey gulf; the mountains are white above and the water dark below, and the way feels like the last way in the world.
Old dwarf-roads and elven paths thread the valleys — ways worn before the world was changed, still trodden by the dwindling folk of the mountains' halls.
Sea-rain drives across the ridges; the old paths run with water, and the mountains are a blue wall hidden in grey mist.
Wind-bent oak and downy birch behind the western dunes, salted and low, facing the open Sea with nothing between here and the horizon.
Fern and moss in the wet hollows; grey light the rest.
The way west along the surf-line — Elf-laid stones half-buried in blown sand, running cape to cape above the thundering beaches.
Shore-paths through the grass-bound dunes and along the high-tide line; wrack and driftwood mark where the last storm reached.
Dark pine and wind-bent oak packed into the ravines that cut the headlands — ancient wood that the gales cannot reach, grey-green and still.
The sea is never more than a short walk away.
The headland road climbs and drops between the capes, grey Elf-stone on the steeps, the sea always filling the western eye.
Paths thread the ravine-woods to the headland tops; from each cape the next stands out dark against the water.
The north-eaves of the Wood — greener and less shadowed than the south, beech-woods over halls of living stone where the Elvenking holds his court beneath the hill.
The beech-woods stand silver and bare; the great doors are shut against the cold, and the fires burn deep under the hill.
Rain on the north-eaves is a green dripping; the Forest River runs full and dark under its bridge, and the air smells of wet earth and old stone.
The green wood is loud with birdsong; feasts in the torch-lit glades go on into the long twilight, and lanterns move like stars under the leaves.
The Forest River runs out of the black woods to the gates of the Elvenking's halls; the road crosses it on a bridge of stone, and beyond the doors there is no road but the river.
Hidden ways thread the green wood to the halls and the deep cellars; the forest here is watched and warded, and the deer-parks are ancient.
Snow lies on the paths to the doors; the deer come down to the frozen river-meadows, and the wood is white and silent.
Scrub of blackthorn and wind-bent birch reclaiming the fallow fields, thickening where the ditches failed.
Old orchards gone wild still bear a sour fruit no one picks.
These are woods that grew where a countryside died.
Bare downs running north toward the marches, watch-towers roofless along the crests.
Grass lies over the plough-ridges of a dead countryside — the man-less lands.
The wind has the hills to itself now, and the wolves.
The roofless towers stand white-shouldered over a dead countryside; the snow fills the old plough-ridges and the marches are very quiet.
Sullen meres stand in the hollows where the drains were let fail, reeds marching over drowned field-lines.
Eel-dark water, unvisited.
Only the rising of wildfowl marks a traveller's passing.
The old war-road runs east toward the marches, hard-kept by patrols and little else.
Its verges grow long and its waystones stand far apart.
Whoever shares it with you is armed, or is no one at all.
Tracks that are more the wolf's and the brigand's than the herdsman's — faint ways between ruined steads, crossing grass-grown furrows.
Cautious folk step light here, and do not stop.
Snow lies unbroken on the war-road; the wolf-tracks cross it where they will.
To walk it is to be the only mark upon a white land.
Rain falls on the man-less lands without witness; the furrows fill, the ruined steads drip, and the wolves go to ground in the thorn.
The empty downs lie iron-hard under frost; breath smokes and sound carries far.
Nothing moves on the war-road but the wind and what hunts in it.
Open moorwood of scattered pine and rowan over deep heather — trees spaced by the wind, more sky than canopy.
Grouse rise underfoot; the quiet here is wide rather than deep.
A high moor-road inland of the cliffs, cairned where the ground is soft, running between the dark pools and the standing stones.
Heather-paths between the pools and the tors; in August the moor goes purple and the bees cloud the walking.
River-valley woods of birch and alder along the cold west-running burns — the green lanes of Forlindon, sheltered and loud with water.
Otters work the pools; kingfisher flashes mark the fords.
The vale road follows the burns down to the sea-lochs, crossing on old Elf-bridges where the water narrows.
Paths along the water and over the high saddles — the valley ways between the pinewoods and the shore.
Sparse silver fir and juniper on the high bare plateau — the last wood before the grey fells, wind-thinned to a fringe.
Below, the sea is a line of light past the headlands.
A fell-road on the high ground, exposed to every weather the west sends, marked with tall cairns against the mist.
Fell-paths over the bare tops and down the burn-gullies; the snow marks lie on them late into spring.
Small copses of ash and birch stand out of the grass like islands, wind-flagged and thin.
Shelter ends where the trees do.
Beyond the last copse there is only the plain and the sky.
The rocky western skirts of the Evendim heights break against the plain — knuckles of grey stone through thin grass.
Hard walking and harder cover.
In the brief summer wildflowers take the meadows and the rocks alike.
The rocky skirts stand grey and bitter; the wildflowers are long gone, and only the wind moves over the stones.
Rain-fed pools lie in the clay hollows, dark for a season and mud by summer's end.
Duck and snipe find them; little else does.
The rest of the year they are only stains in the grass.
The west road runs long and empty toward the Vale of the Lhun and the Elven lands beyond.
Under a very wide sky its waystones stand far apart.
The wind keeps the crown of it swept clean.
Faint grass tracks between the copses and the meadows, made more by deer than men.
Easy to follow, easier to lose.
Nothing marks the way here but the flowers and the wind.
The drear plain takes the rain without shelter; the grass streams, the clay-pools spread, and the copses drip for days after.
A clear hard cold locks the plain; the frost-cracked pools shine like glass and the wind off the tundra takes the feeling from your face.
Crouched birch and willow in the stream-gullies, wind-carved and knee-bent — the last wood before the Waste.
Beyond the plateau's edge no tree dares stand.
The dry northern plateau rises empty into a sky without end, moor-edge and stone where Arthedain stops and the Wash begins.
Beacon-tors stand unlit on the high points.
Nothing between here and the tundra breaks the wind.
Winter owns the plateau outright; the beacon-tors stand white and empty, and the wind does what it will with the drifts.
Bog-pools black as slate lie in the peat hags, frozen half the year and bottomless-looking the other half.
Moss and sedge, and the cry of a single curlew.
The ground speaks softly underfoot and takes the careless.
The last military road of the north runs to the wall-forts, cairned and drained for patrols that come rarer every year.
Past its end there is no road at all.
Patrol-paths along the plateau edge, marked with small cairns where the ground is stone.
Beyond them only the Wash and the wolves know the way.
The snow takes these marks early and keeps them late.
Cold rain blows level across the plateau; the peat runs with black water and the cairns loom and vanish in the wet.
The plateau hardens into silence; the bog-pools film with ice, and the wind comes down off the Wash like a blade.
Snow covers the cairns and fills the gullies; the patrol-paths vanish, and beyond the wall-forts the Waste and the land are one white thing.
Rain drips through the birch and rowan; the alder along the lake-streams stands dark and wet, and the mist does not lift.
Birch and rowan over thin stony soil, alder along the streams that run down to the lake.
Quiet groves, light-dappled, where the shepherds cut their winter fodder.
The woods hold the lake-mist till mid-morning.
The Hills of Twilight stand white above a white shore; Annúminas shows its grey walls against the snow, and the shepherds keep to the lower vales.
The Hills of Twilight — long rolling heights of green-grey turf, stone-walled fields running up the easy slopes.
Below, Lake Nenuial lies silver and wide, and on its shore Annúminas stands empty in the light.
The barrows of the first kings look down on all of it.
Lake-margin fens where Nenuial's waters meet the reed — waterfowl in thousands, mist standing over the flats at dawn.
The drowned quiet of a shore that once held a city of kings.
The old royal way west toward Annúminas runs grass-grown but true beneath the turf, built when the seat of kings was here.
Sheep use it now, and travellers who know a pavement when they feel it underfoot.
Rain comes down off the heights into the stone-walled fields; the lake-mist thickens, the shepherd-paths run wet, and Nenuial disappears into grey.
Frost sparkles on the stone walls; the sheep are folded low, and below the hills the lake lies steel-coloured and still.
Shepherd-paths between stone-walled fields, worn thin over stony soil, running down to the lake's grey margin.
Long easy miles under a wide sky.
The mist finds these paths first and leaves them last.
Copses of ash and rowan on the downs above the Nin Erain, kept once as royal hunting coverts.
Old mine-workings sleep beneath the roots, and gnarled hawthorn marks where the shafts were.
The wood keeps its own counsel.
Fornost stands grey above a white country; the quarries and the old shafts are rimed, and Norland's Glower is bleak with driven snow.
The North Downs proper — and over all, Norland's Glower, where the grey walls of Fornost crown the highest crest.
Gorse and cropped turf below, quarries and tin-workings older than the kingdom.
From the tops the land falls away on every side to a very great sky.
Peat-pools and bog in the high vales where the Nin Erain is young, black water cupped between the downs.
Curlews cry over them.
The cold sits in these hollows long after the hills are warm.
The royal road shines wet between the downs; the carts go slower, the mile-stones drip, and the gates of Fornost come blurred out of the rain.
The royal road to Fornost — broad fitted stone running up between the downs to the gates, mile-stones cut with the Seven Stars.
Tin and lead come down it, grain and soldiery go up.
The busiest way north of the White Downs.
Rain runs off the downs in sheets; the mine-headings drip, the gorse is flattened dark, and the walls of Fornost blur into the weather.
A hard frost grips the North Downs; the peat-pools film, the turf rings underfoot, and smoke from the city hangs level in the still air.
Paths between the downs' farms and the old mine-headings, sheep-worn and sure, climbing to the crests and the observatory ridge.
Waymarks at the forking.
The wind at the top explains why they built high.
Bare black branches net the grey sky, and the floor is a drift of wet leaves over hidden roots.
The cold seeps upward like a held breath.
A wall of ancient trees — oak and ash and gnarled willow grown so close that daylight fails among them.
The air is still and watchful; moisture drips without wind, and a shout returns muffled, with no answer.
Rain sifts down through the close leaves in a fine cold drizzle; every trunk glistens black and the drip of water fills the silence.
The wood seems pleased, and deepens around the path.
Even at midsummer the heat dies at the eaves; within, the air is green, dim and cool, smelling of leaf-mould and damp bark.
The old path is a mire of half-frozen leaves; the trees crowd closer in the pale light, and the way seems shorter each time it is sought.
No true road runs under the eaves — only the old paths that the Forest tolerates, narrow ways that shift and fade between one visit and the next.
Frost finds little purchase under the boughs, but a damp chill works through cloth and leather alike; the mist of the valley clings cold to the skin.
The paths wind among huge roots and fallen boughs, doubling back as if the wood itself misdirected the feet.
In the deep dells a stream murmurs over wild herbs, and the willows creak and rustle though no wind stirs.
A mixed land more than a wood: fertile lowland plains and pasture broken by ragged copses of oak and birch, the thinned remnant of older forest.
Harsh winds scour the uplands while the river-vales lie green and tilled, dotted with the heath and bracken reclaiming abandoned ground.
Low chalk-and-turf downs rolling to the horizon, dotted with ancient barrows and crowned here and there by weathered stone.
Open, windswept, and brooding over the old graves.

A weathered stretch of the Great North Road, once proud and now patched and rutted, its milestones toppled; still used by merchant caravans that move in numbers, wary of the empty leagues between towns.
A faint field-path through heath and old pasture, easy to lose where the bracken has swallowed it, threading between grass-grown barrows.
Groves of oak and beech clothe the lower slopes — a fair field of trees above the grassland, green in spring and russet after the turning.
The groves stand leafless and the brown drifts of mast lie deep; the paths are silent but for the drip of the thaw.
Rolling downs above the Anduin vales — turf thick underfoot and grave-mounds green where older folk sleep under the grass.
The field lies bare and brown; the wind comes down off the mountains with ice in it, and the grass is stiff with frost.
Rain sweeps the open field; the grass lies flat and shining, and the old mounds stand dark in the wet.
The cold crowns of the world stand beyond the dale — close enough to touch the sight though far to reach, remote and bright.
The southern spurs of the Misty Mountains fall away in grey ridges toward the field, their feet clothed in dark pine.
High shoulders of the range look down on the field; on clear days the snow on the far peaks burns white against the sky.
The old road of the North Kingdom runs through the field — its line still clear under the grass, marking where an army once broke and a realm was lost.
The road-line lies under summer grass and flowers; larksong is everywhere and the field is a green sea moving in the wind.
Green trails cross the field between the groves; the grass is soft underfoot and the larks are loud in the high air.
The green ways are hard under frost; the air is keen and the view to the mountains is bright and cold as drawn steel.
A mixed land more than a wood: fertile lowland plains and pasture broken by ragged copses of oak and birch, the thinned remnant of older forest.
Harsh winds scour the uplands while the river-vales lie green and tilled, dotted with the heath and bracken reclaiming abandoned ground.
Low chalk-and-turf downs rolling to the horizon, dotted with ancient barrows and crowned here and there by weathered stone.
Open, windswept, and brooding over the old graves.

A weathered stretch of the Great North Road, once proud and now patched and rutted, its milestones toppled; still used by merchant caravans that move in numbers, wary of the empty leagues between towns.
A faint field-path through heath and old pasture, easy to lose where the bracken has swallowed it, threading between grass-grown barrows.
Scrub and stunted trees grow in dense patches between barren spaces — hawthorn, briar and wind-bent ash.
In the thickets grows kingsfoil, sweetening the air where a leaf is crushed.
The thickets are brittle with frost and the grey grass is stiff underfoot; nothing moves in the scrub but the wind, searching.
West winds drive fine, soaking rain onto the dark hills; the ridges run with water and the stones are black and streaming.
Snow lies thin and dirty on the northern slopes, and the wind off the high moor cuts like a drawn blade; the ruined walls give no shelter.
The cold comes down off the hills at dusk; sparse grass and withered leaves barely stir, and every hollow holds its own shadow and its own chill.
A long line of ancient hills marching north and south, crowned here and there with the ringed ruins of old watch-towers.
Weathertop stands highest — bare, windy, and commanding all the Road below.
In the low ground east of the ridge the Midgewater Marshes stretch flat and reedy — pools, sedge, and the cries of hidden birds under a wide grey sky.
The East Road runs along the western feet of the hills — the last true way before the wild.
From the ridges it shows pale and lonely under the sky.
Rain curtains the hills and turns the Road's verge to black mud; the land runs with whispering water, and the towers stand unseen in the murk.
Faint paths thread the heather and stone of the heights, made more by sheep and weather than by feet; south of the Road the ground is trackless scrub and thicket.
The woodlands of the Mark are the eaves of Fangorn's skirts on the north and dark fir in the mountain dales; the Westfold's groves are windbreaks of beech on the farms.
The fir-woods of the dales stand black under snow; the wind seethes in them, and the green eaves of Fangorn's edge are dark and still.
The high snows stand over the Mark like a second sky — Starkhorn and Irensaga and the Dwimorberg, the haunted peak where the Dark Door waits in the mountain's root.
The foothills of the White Mountains rise steep and green behind Edoras — long grass slopes where the horse-herds graze beneath the high white wall.
Snow lies on the green foothills and the dales are white between black fir-woods; the Snowbourn runs dark and loud under icy banks.
The Ered Nimrais make the southern wall of the Mark — a white rampart from Dunharrow to the Isen, with the deep green gorge of Harrowdale cleft into their feet.
The White Mountains stand to their waists in snow; the high pastures are buried, and the wind off the peaks brings ice-dust down to the dales.
The Riddermark — a sea of grass from the Entwash to the mountain wall, empty and wide under a huge sky.
The wind never rests on it, and the distant riders are small as dust.
The plains lie pale and sere under the winter sky; a thin searching wind comes down off the northern snows, and the grass is grey as the manes of horses.
The grassland stands high and green-gold; the wind moves through it like a tide, and larks sing invisible in the warm blue air.
Rain sweeps the open Mark in long grey veils; the grass lies flat and shining, and the horizon is a wall of moving water.
A keen cold rides the plains; the wind out of the north comes unhindered across a hundred miles of frozen grass.
The roads of the Mark are green ways beaten by hooves — the road to Edoras under its green hill, and the west road running along the mountain wall toward the Fords of Isen.
The road to Edoras lies pale and hard under frost; the green hill of Meduseld stands grey above it, and the Golden Hall's thatch is dull under the cold sky.
Horse-paths cross the open grass in every direction; in the dales the tracks climb beside rushing streams to the high pastures and the hidden refuges.
The hill-tracks are white lines in the sere grass; the dale-streams are rimed at their edges, and the high refuges are cold and empty.
Sparse woods of birch and thorn stand on the northern slopes; toward the east the great dark line of Fangorn's eaves marks the land's end.
The birch-woods stand white and bare; the tracks are lost in drifted grass, and the dark line of Fangorn is blurred by falling snow.
A grey cold lies on the Wold; the land is a frozen sea of pale grass, and the dark of Fangorn is a black wall on the horizon.
The Wold is a high rolling grassland — lonelier and wilder than the fields of the south, empty downs where the northern herds graze and the wind has the run of the sky.
The Wold lies sere and empty; frost whitens the long grass and the northern wind drives thin snow across the open downs.
No true roads cross the Wold — only the green tracks of the Riders going north to the downs, and the old path toward the Fords of the Entwash.
The green tracks are hard under frost; the way north is an empty line between white field and grey sky.
Grass tracks wind over the rolling uplands; eastward they fade where the dark forest begins and the land falls away to the Entwash's banks.
Rain drives over the open downs; the grass-tracks run with water and the mist hides the dark eaves of the forest to the east.
Sheltered haven-woods of oak and hazel behind the still bays — the gentlest wood in Forlindon, where the sea comes in quiet and green.
Swan and heron work the shallows below the trees.
The haven road runs from landing to landing, past the grey quays where the Elven boats still come and go.
Paths along the sheltered strand and through the wood to the quays; on still evenings the water holds the light long after the hills go dark.
Young birch and rowan over the old burnt fell — pale pioneer wood reclaiming land that stood bare for an age.
Bright-leaved and thin, green against the grey stone.
An open road across the young wood and the bare fell, the Gulf of Lhun always visible to the south, white under the sky.
Paths through the pale birch-stands, airy and quick to walk; in autumn the whole country goes gold at once.
Cold, sparse stands of hardy pine and birch on the bleak northern skirts of Gundabad, wind-stripped and snow-streaked, thinning fast into bare rock.
The lower skirts of Mount Gundabad, bare grey stone and tundra-grass swept by an endless cold wind, snow lingering in the hollows of a grim orc-haunted height.
A harsh orc-trodden way through the cold northern uplands below Gundabad, unpaved and menacing, kept by the enemy rather than by any free folk.
A harsh trace over cold stone below Gundabad, orc-trodden and mean, that gives out among the boulders.
At the edge of the Plain of Everlasting Cold, only dwarf-birch and creeping pine survive in sheltered hollows before the tundra takes all.
Frost-stunted and sparse under a wide pale sky.
No made road; a bleak route across the frozen plain marked by rare cairns, swept bare by the wind and lost under drifting snow.
A faint line across the frozen plain, read from drift and cairn, that the next wind will scour away.
The great peaks of the north — bare stone and permanent snow, cleft by the passes where the paths go in and do not all come out.
The goblins' doors are hidden in the rocks.
The northern peaks stand deep in winter long after the vales are green; avalanches growl in the gullies, and the passes are a white silence.
Cold rules the heights; even the eagles keep their eyries close, and the wind off the ice-fields numbs the air it touches.
The forest edge climbs into broken foothills of pine and scree; above them the bare rock rises in walls and chimneys toward the passes.
Rain brings the hillsides down in wet cascades; the paths to the pass are running streams, and the shelters of the rocks are black with damp.
High grey slopes where the great eagles have their eyries, looking down over oak and elm woods and the River winding far below.
Storms rake the high slopes; water pours off the crags in silver threads, and the caves of the pass drip and echo.
The High Pass climbs by caves and rock-gates; a dry shelter in a storm may be a doorway to the dark, and the goblin-gate opens where the path seems safest.
Narrow paths climb from the woods to the wolf-haunted heights; the eagles' road is the wind, and it is not for walking.
The winter paths are buried; the way is marked only by the line of the crags, and wolves follow what the snow conceals.
Cold pine and spruce on the mountain skirts, dark and resinous, the needled floor muffling every step.
Mist pools between the trunks; old boundary-stones and broken walls of lost Arnor surface among the roots.
Stony upland shoulders rising toward the High Pass, grass and lichen over grey rock, strewn with the rubble of old watch-towers and the boundary-marks of a lost realm.
A faint remnant of a Dunadan road climbing toward the High Pass, its stones scattered and grass-grown, more memory of a road than a road itself.
A faint upland trace among the pines, marked by cairns half-fallen, that fades into scree near the high places.
Cultivated, Mediterranean woodland: groves of holm-oak, chestnut and cypress give way to olive and almond on the warmer slopes, with orchards and flowering vales.
The undergrowth is aromatic with broom, thyme and rockrose; tended, sunlit, prosperous woods.
Fertile foothills of the White Mountains, terraced with vine and olive and laced with clear streams.
Warm and sunlit, the green skirts where mountain meets tilled land.
Dry southern steppe of bleached grass and thornscrub, shimmering with heat, rolling flat and vast toward the unknown east.
A well-kept Gondorian road of fitted stone, straight and sure, with drainage and standing waymarks; the traffic of trade and soldiery keeps it busy and its verges clear.
A trodden countryside path between orchards and terraces, sun-warm and clear, worn smooth by shepherds and farmhands.
A cold clear dawn reveals the holly-hills crowned with dark leaves and red berries, and the snowy mountain-peaks stand ahead beyond them.
The wind drops and the land holds its breath.
Low holly-trees crown the stony hills — Hollin the Elves called this land, for the hollies that were its mark.
Their dark leaves catch the sun and their berries glow red as drops of blood on a clear day.
Bare ridges and long slopes of broken stone rise toward the mountain wall.
From the high ground the three peaks of Moria stand ahead between the drifting clouds.
Snow lies on the high ridges of Eregion and clouds blow low across the passes.
The holly shows black against the white slopes and the land is silent.
The wind drops and shifts at dawn and the cold is sharp and clear; every stone casts a blue shadow, and the air smells of the high snows.
The old Elven road runs west of the mountains toward the buried doors — grass-grown and rutted now, but its line is still true under the heather, and it ends at the Walls of Moria.
The old road is a pale line under frost; the holly-berries are the only red thing in a white and silent land, and the mountains ahead are walls of winter.
Paths follow the old watercourses toward the mountain's feet; the Sirannon's bed is a thread of brown, red-stained stones, and no bird moves in the empty sky above it.
Rain sweeps over the bare ridges and runs in the dry courses of the streams; for an hour the dead land drinks, then is barren and silent again.
The horn of Caradhras rises into a world of storm; snow and ice lash its shoulders, and thunder rolls through its hollows when the mountain is angry.
On the high slopes the snow falls thick and blinding; the wind heaps it in the clefts, and the mountain seems to breathe a white malice.
The cold on Caradhras is beyond frost and wind; it is a hatred in the stone itself, and no fire at its feet will warm it.
Barren foothills of red and grey stone, cut by the dry beds of streams that once ran bright.
The bones of the great city lie beneath, and the hills keep their counsel.
Rain fills the empty stream-beds for an hour and the hills run with sudden water; then the channels fall silent and red-stained again.
Three peaks stand over the hidden doors — Caradhras cruel and tall, Celebdil, and Fanuidhol — and below them the Dimrill Dale lies silent around the dark water of Mirrormere.
Snow closes over the Dimrill Dale and the Stair; the passes fill with drifting white, and the peaks above are lost in storm.
Winter wraps the Dale in deep snow and Mirrormere lies black and still, reflecting only the stars and the shoulders of the peaks.
The road to the West-gate climbs by the black mere and the last hollies, ending at sheer cliffs and doors that have been shut a thousand years.
Rough tracks cross the Dimrill Dale beside Mirrormere's dark water; the Dimrill Stair climbs the falls beside them, worn by feet that are long gone.
The trail to the Stair vanishes under drifted snow; the way is memory and guesswork between white walls of stone.
The old forests of Dunland are gone — felled for the fires of Isengard.
Stumps and a few bitter brakes remain on the hills; the surviving woods stand far and sparse, and the people remember the trees.
The stump-dotted hills stand black under frost; what woods remain are dark and still, and the land is bitter and bare.
Green hills and long empty downs — a proud, poor country that remembers when it was richer.
The hill-men keep their own speech, their own ways, and their old grievances against the strawheads of the valleys.
The downs are brown and bare; the wind out of the Gap is keen, and the hill-steads send up thin grey smoke against the cold.
A hard cold sits on Dunland; the smoke of the stead-fires lies flat, and the wind off Methedras is a whetted edge.
Methedras stands at the range's end — the last horn of the mountains, snow-capped and looking down on the vale of the traitor and the tower that casts a shadow like a hand.
The foothills of the Misty Mountains rise bare to the west, cut by the gorges of the Isen; the rock is grey and close, and the river runs loud between the walls.
Snow lies deep on the foothills and the gorges of the Isen are white; the passes above are closed and silent.
The southern Misty Mountains wall the west — grey heights where the passes of the Gap run up into cloud, and the last peaks look down on the ring of Isengard.
Rain sweeps the Gap and the old road runs wet under the mountains' wall; the Isen comes down loud and brown and the fords run deep.
The old North-South Road runs down from the Gap of Rohan past the ring of Isengard — once the road of two kingdoms, now a way watched and uneasy, with ruined holdings beside it.
Hill-paths cross the downs to the hidden steads of the Dunlendings; the tracks are many and secret, and the eyes that watch from the ridges are not friendly.
The hill-paths are rivulets; rain drives across the empty downs and the secret ways are grey threads in the wet.
Thin boreal taiga of stunted spruce and pine, lichen-draped and snow-bent, surrendering quickly to open tundra.
The trees grow low and hard and the silence is glacial.
Low snow-streaked tundra-hills of bare rock and frozen moss, wind-scoured and treeless under a pale northern sky.
Frozen fen and bog along the icebound shore, half-marsh half-tundra, meltwater pooling between hummocks of frozen moss where every step is a cold labour.
No made road at all; a route across the snow marked by cairns and whale-bone stakes, followed by sled and by foot, that vanishes with each fresh fall.
No trail but a line of footprints soon erased, a route read from the shape of the snow and the set of the wind by those who know the ice.
When rain comes to the inner country it falls black and hot through the fumes; the ash turns to black mud and the thorn-brakes steam.
Scrub and thorn where anything grows at all — grey brambles and stunted bitter trees in the crevices of the Morgai.
Nothing green lives long here; the briars claw like wire.
Cold pools in the ravines of the Morgai; the scree is stiff with frost and the jagged ridges ring in the freezing air.
The Morgai — a harsh maze of broken slopes and ravines, sliding scree and jagged ridges, the inner mountain-wall where the last life gives way to bare stone.
The heat comes off the plain in waves; the ash-shimmer hides the distances and the fume of Orodruin hangs red and heavy.
Thirst is a torment here.
Winter in Gorgoroth is a cold more bitter than the heat — black frost on the slag, and wind off the mountains that cuts through every rag.
Gorgoroth — a plateau of ash and slag under a roof of fume.
The ground is broken by pits and mounds, the air is bitter and drying, and water is a precious, guarded thing.
Broad orc-roads cross the plain, laid straight and dreary between the forts and the furnace-pits; the dust of them hangs in the air and the way is marked by ruin.
The roads bake under the dim red sun; dust rises from the marching columns and the iron ruts shine like heated wire.
The dust lies frozen in the ruts; the way is iron-hard and the cold wind drives black sleet across the empty miles.
The ravine-paths are fanged with black ice; the cold climbs out of the depths and the stone bites the hand that holds it.
Paths climb the ravines of the Morgai by ledges and hidden stairs — ways made for war and watching, hard and bare and cruel.
The woods thin toward the Morgul Vale — dark ilex and ash, and pale silent groves where the light seems poisoned.
Near the Cross-roads the trees stand as if listening for the enemy's drums.
The pale woods drip with cold dew; the leaves hang limp and black, and the Morgul-mist creeps among the trunks like a living thing.
The northern hills are steep and wild, cleft by the black cleft of the Morgul Vale.
White pinnacles and broken towers look down on a land that was once all gardens.
Cold seeps out of the Vale; the white pinnacles are sharp in the freezing air, and the stream below steams like a breath in the cold.
The hills stand bare and colourless; ice rims the pools of the Morgulduin and the dead white flowers nod in the cold meadows.
The wraith-road comes down out of the Vale to meet the Harad Road at the Cross-roads — a pale way between the dead city and the land of shadow.
A broken statue of a king keeps watch there, crowned now with trailing flowers.
Rain falls thin and cold on the haunted road; the carved king's crown of flowers is beaten down with wet, and the white stone glistens.
Stair-paths cut between sheer faces of rock climb the western wall of the Vale — the Straight Stair and the Winding Stair, narrow, cracked by forgotten winters, and watched from above.
Ice glazes the narrow stairs; the crevices hold old snow, and the red glow above is blurred by cold mist.
A few grey, struggling stands of hardy scrub and dead-looking trees cling to the shores of the bitter inland sea, half-alive under a smoke-stained sky.
Little more than the memory of a forest.
Brackish salt-fens along the Sea of Nurnen, grey and reeking, where slave-worked channels cut through salt-reed and mud under a smoke-stained sky.
The lower volcanic ridges above the Sea of Nurnen, grey-brown and barren but less utterly dead than the north, where slave-fields scrape what little the bitter soil allows.
Grudging grey fields along the bitter sea, salt-crusted and slave-worked, flat and joyless under a smoke-stained sky.
A slave-road of beaten earth along the bitter sea, rutted by the carts that haul Nurn's grudging harvest north to feed the armies of the Dark Tower.
A slave-worn path between the salt-fields and the shore, churned and bitter, watched from the ridges by the overseers.
Twisted, tangled woods of the rugged uplands, ancient and deserted: gnarled oak and thorn-brake over broken stony ground, home now only to scattered Druedain and Dunlending bands.
A wild, depopulated march where the forest has crept back over abandoned Gondorian land.
Fertile foothills of the White Mountains, terraced with vine and olive and laced with clear streams.
Warm and sunlit, the green skirts where mountain meets tilled land.
The high White Mountains, the Ered Nimrais, crowned with perpetual snow and glacier above the treeline.
Knife-edged ridges and sheer pale walls blaze in the sun; the cold is absolute, the silence broken only by wind and distant ice.
The green foothills of the White Mountains, terraced with olive and vine where they meet the lowlands, laced with shepherd-paths and tumbling brooks.
Warm, fertile and sunlit, the gentlest face of the great range.
The middle slopes of the Ered Nimrais, where forest yields to alpine meadow and grey crag.
Cloud snags on the ridges, streams fall in white threads, and the air thins and chills as the green runs out into stone.

The woods of Anorien are the tended groves of the north — planted beech and fir on the foothills of the White Mountains, cut and grown again for the City's timber.
Eastward the old Drúadan Forest stands wild and dark on the mountain's knees.
The fir-woods on the foothills stand black and quiet under a weight of frost.
The snow creaks under the boughs and the resin-smell is sharp and cold.
The beacon-hills march along the mountain feet — Amon Dîn, Eilenach, Nardol, Erelas, Min-Rimmon, Calenhad, and green Halifirien last and highest.
Below them the land rolls down in long open slopes to the fields of the Pelennor.
The beacon-hills stand grey and bare; the high pastures are stiff with frost and the signal-wood is stacked dark against the sky.
On clear days the whole line of peaks burns white to the south.
High and remote the great peaks stand in their snows; even at midsummer the air off them is cool, and they catch the first and last light like a row of lit beacons.
The foothills of Ered Nimrais rise steep above the plain — grass slopes and pine-woods under the white wall, where snow lingers late and cold streams run down out of the heights.
Snow lies deep on the foothill pastures and the pine-woods carry it in white folds.
The streams run dark and loud between icy banks.
The White Mountains fill the southern sky — a rampart of grey cliff and snowfield, Mindolluin nearest and tallest over the City.
The wind that comes down off them at evening smells of stone and ice.
The White Mountains are a frozen wall; their snow reaches down into the fir-woods, and Mindolluin stands over the City like the king of winter.
The Pelennor is a fenced green field between mountain and river — dykes and orchards, tilth and meadow, all within sight of the City walls.
Beyond the wall the land rises into the fair empty hills of the north.
Midsummer lies golden on the Pelennor — hay high in the fields, bees in the linden-rows, and the City walls shining in the long light.
The orchards hang heavy and the dykes run slow and green.
Rain on the Pelennor is warm and fruitful; the dykes run full, the orchards shine, and the City stands grey-gold through the veil.
The Great West Road runs from the City through the green townlands and away north toward the fords of the Isen and the fields of the Mark.
Its stones are worn by hooves and by the passage of armies.
Rain falls soft on the green townlands; the West Road shines wet and the beacon-hills are dim islands in the mist.
The orchards drip and the fields drink.
Drove-roads and field-paths cross the farms; on the foothills the old paths of the mountain-men climb through the fir-woods to the beacon-tops.
Cold comes down the mountain paths at dusk; the beacon-tops are icy and the air off the high snows bites the hands that tend the warning-fires.
Pines on the high moors and a tumble of birch, beech and rowan down the steep valley sides; in the hidden valley below, the woods are green and sweet even in late autumn.
Golden light lies long on the valley woods; the Bruinen murmurs under the eaves, and the air is sweet with leaf and bloom.
The pines seethe and sigh under a streaming east wind; below in the valley the sheltered boughs hold their green, and the sound of the falls comes up muffled through the cold.
The high moor above the valley is bare and windswept heath; the valley itself is a deep-cleft green refuge that the hills conceal from every side.
The Road comes down from the moors by steep stony ways, and where the valley is reached it ends — as all journeys here end — at the Last Homely House.
Cold rain slants down the moor and turns the stony way to a shining thread; in the valley the river's voice swells until the hills ring with it.
An east wind streams through bare branches and seethes in the dark pines beneath low, ragged clouds; the river roars among the stones, and the grey of December lies on the moor.
Paths climb between the pines and drop to the ford, where the Bruinen's loud water is the first voice of the valley.
Higher up the tracks are for deer and for those who know them.
The warm evening air smells of trees and flowers; running water sounds in the valley below, and it seems that summer lingers here beyond its time.
A westerly wind brings cold rain through the hills, driving the last yellow leaves across the path; below, the Bruinen runs loud and wild and mist closes over the valley mouth.
Thin woods of alder and thorn stand in the wet bottoms, and scrub creeps up the stony ridges.
The trees are sparse and old — survivors of a land that was once all farms and fields.
Rain whispers in the thin woods and drips from bare alder twigs; the ground under the trees is black and soft and smells of rot.
Low rolling hills of tussock and thorn under a wide empty sky.
